subsections.title: Overview
subsections.summary: What it is and why it matters.

blocks.html: Most messages, emails and calls pass through a company's servers on the way. With ordinary SMS and email, that company — and anyone it hands data to — can read them. End-to-end encrypted apps like Signal mean only you and the person you're talking to can read the content, and email aliases stop your real address from spreading.

subsections.title: Terminology
subsections.summary: The words you will run into.

items.title: End-to-end encryption (E2EE)
items.html: Only the people in the conversation can read it — not the app, not the carrier.

items.title: Metadata
items.html: Who you talked to, when and for how long. Even encrypted apps may see this.

items.title: Email alias
items.html: A forwarding address that hides your real one. Use a new one per site.

items.title: VoIP
items.html: Voice over IP — calls made over the internet instead of the phone network.

items.title: Disappearing messages
items.html: Messages that delete themselves after a set time.

subsections.title: Choosing a Tool
subsections.summary: What to look for in any messenger or email service.

items.title: Encrypted by default
items.html: End-to-end encryption should be on for every chat and call, not an option you have to find.

items.title: No phone number needed
items.html: A phone number ties an account to your real identity. Some apps work without one, or let you hide it behind a username.

items.title: Open source & audited
items.html: Public code and independent security audits mean you don’t have to take the company’s word for it.

items.title: Disappearing messages
items.html: Messages that delete themselves protect you if a phone is lost, seized or hacked later.

items.title: Little metadata
items.html: Even when content is encrypted, who you talk to and when can be revealing. Prefer services that keep as little as possible.

items.title: Who runs the server
items.html: For self-hosted and federated tools (Matrix, Jitsi, Mastodon), the person running your server can see more. Pick one you trust.

blocks.label: WhatsApp & Telegram
blocks.html: WhatsApp encrypts message content but shares metadata with Meta. Telegram’s normal and group chats aren’t end-to-end encrypted, so Telegram itself can read them. Both are fine for public channels; use Signal or SimpleX for anything private.

subsections.title: Aliases & Disposable Email
subsections.summary: Keep your real address out of sign-up forms.

blocks.html: Use an alias for accounts you’ll keep — it forwards to your inbox and can be switched off if it starts getting spam. Use a disposable inbox only for one-off sign-ups you never need again.

blocks.label: Careful
blocks.html: Many disposable inboxes are public: anyone who types the same address can read the mail. Never use one for an account you care about — whoever uses that address next could reset your password.

subsections.title: Run Your Own Email
subsections.summary: Self-hosted mail servers — and why it’s hard.

blocks.html: Running your own mail server gives you full control, but it is one of the hardest things to self-host. Big providers reject mail without correct SPF, DKIM and DMARC records, new servers often land on blocklists, and many home internet providers block the ports email needs. DIY Mail is an honest look at what it takes. If you just want your own domain, a host like Migadu or MXroute is far easier.

subsections.title: Social Media
subsections.summary: Safer settings, and platforms without an algorithm.

items.text: Review the privacy settings on every account you have
items.details: Platforms change them often. Limit who can see your posts, friends list, birthday and contact details.

items.text: Share less about where you are
items.details: Turn off location tagging, post after you’ve left a place, and strip location data from photos before posting.

items.text: Use the website instead of the app
items.details: Apps can collect contacts, location and device data that a browser tab can’t.

items.text: Keep separate accounts for separate parts of your life
items.details: Work, personal and activism accounts shouldn’t share a phone number or email.

items.text: Move private groups off big platforms
items.details: Use Signal or Delta Chat for small trusted groups, and a mailing list or Mastodon for announcements.

subsections.title: If an Account Is Hacked
subsections.summary: Signs of compromise and what to do first.

blocks.html: Signs: settings or posts you didn’t change, contacts getting messages you didn’t send, your correct password being rejected, password-reset emails you didn’t ask for, or logins from places you’ve never been.

items.title: Stop using it for anything sensitive
items.text: Until you know what happened, assume someone else can read the account.

items.title: Change the password
items.text: Use a new, unique password from your password manager, and change it anywhere else you used the same one.

items.title: Sign out every other session
items.text: Find the account’s list of active sessions or devices and log out of everything you don’t recognise.

items.title: Check forwarding and recovery settings
items.text: Look for email forwarding rules, recovery emails or phone numbers you didn’t add — attackers use them to keep access.

items.title: Turn on two-factor authentication
items.text: Use an authenticator app or security key. See Auth / 2FA.

items.title: Unlink connected apps
items.text: Remove “Sign in with Google/Facebook/Apple” connections you don’t use, starting with financial and sensitive accounts.

items.title: Check your devices
items.text: Any phone or computer that was signed in could be the source. Update it and check for apps you don’t recognise.

items.title: Can’t get back in?
items.text: Use the service’s recovery process, then the Digital First Aid Kit. At-risk people can get free help from Access Now’s Digital Security Helpline.
